questions.prompt: A syllogism, in this lecture’s definition, is any argument with:
choices: A Exactly one premise and a joke.
B Two premises and a conclusion.
C An unlimited number of conclusions and no premises.
D Only hypothetical if-then sentences.
questions.explain: Two premises + a conclusion; types include categorical, hypothetical, and disjunctive.

questions.prompt: Validity, as Hicks rehearses it for syllogisms, concerns:
choices: A Whether each premise matches extra-logical facts (biology, etc.).
B The structure/pattern/form of the move from premises to conclusion.
C Whether the speaker is famous.
D Whether the conclusion is popular.
questions.explain: Truth of premises is largely other fields’ job; logic specializes in the formal pattern—valid or invalid.

questions.prompt: A sound argument, the “gold standard” here, is one that has:
choices: A True premises and valid reasoning.
B Valid form even with all false premises, and nothing else.
C True premises even if the inference is a non sequitur.
D Latin names regardless of form.
questions.explain: Both virtues: true incoming information and good logic. That combination is called sound.

questions.prompt: Why can “All rabbits are birds; all birds eat whales; so all rabbits eat whales” still be valid?
choices: A Because the premises are true.
B Because, supposing the premises, the conclusion would follow—the pattern matches the true “humans/mammals/mortal” case.
C Because medieval monks forbade talking about rabbits.
D Because it is a disjunctive syllogism.
questions.explain: Validity ignores actual truth of the contents; the structure is the same as the good mammal example (later named Barbara).

questions.prompt: The middle term in a categorical syllogism is the term that:
choices: A Appears in both premises (the linking term).
B Appears only in the conclusion.
C Is always an either-or connective.
D Must be a proper name like Aristotle.
questions.explain: The middle term appears in both premises. Hicks also notes a rule of thumb about not leaving it only in the predicate twice.
